# Direct the work, don't type it: what a course catalog for AI-era engineers says about a system that runs itself

*An Ultrastable white paper. Ultrastable is the foundation for any autonomous system.*

## Executive summary

Many people believe that with AI agents, the hard part of building software is writing the code, and the skill to learn is a tool. This paper argues otherwise: the code is the cheap half. The work is the spec, the boundary and the check. A person can learn those calls, and a system can encode them: every item says what done means, what is out of scope and what number should move.

unlearn.dev teaches people the calls that sit around an AI agent: what to build, what to leave out, what to reject. Ultrastable makes the same calls with code. We take each lesson, name the old idea it repeats (Toyota's stop-the-line, lean's build-measure-learn, continuous discovery, eval-driven AI work, Ashby's requisite variety) and test whether this system already does it. Where it does not, the gap is a number.

It is written for people who build or run AI systems and want them to keep working without someone watching. It names 5 concrete problems, the mechanism that answers each one, and how to put that mechanism in place.

## 1. The problem

The site's pitch is "Direct AI. Don't get led by it." Agents made typing nearly free, so the skill left is deciding what to build, writing it down so an agent cannot misread it, saying what not to build, and rejecting output that only looks right. Not related to Ultrastable's own Unlearn tenant, which is an evidence encyclopedia of popular beliefs. [1]

This matters now because the usual answer, the skill is the tool; the work is the code, sends teams after the wrong fix. A better model or another reviewer does not close a loop that nothing checks.

The problems in detail:

1. A spec an agent can't misread. Course: plan before you prompt; turn a vague idea into a spec with roles and constraints so the agent "doesn't have to guess". Same idea as lean's hypothesis-first build and eval-driven AI work. Test: every open work item names its done check and a prediction that can fail. [1]
2. Say what must not be built. Course: write down what the system must not build and what a feature excludes, so the agent does not wander. Same idea as scope boundaries in Shape Up and Toyota's standard work. Test: open items carry an Out of scope line. [1]
3. Code that looks right. Course: "AI code looks right, and that's what makes it dangerous"; review by claim, verify, trace, with a second agent. Same idea as Toyota's stop-the-line and Ashby's point that only variety can absorb variety: the check has to be as varied as the change. Test: deploys proven live against their commit. [1]
4. From seems fine to measured. Course: test AI features with evals, from "seems fine" to measured quality. Same idea as continuous discovery and kaizen: no change without a number to judge it. Test: every loop declares a closing probe. [1]
5. An agent you can walk away from. Course: small focused branches, guardrails and hooks before the agent writes code, so its work can be left alone. Test: few changes on main have to be reverted. [1]

## 2. The approach

The approach follows Ashby's ultrastable system [2]: a first loop acts on the world, and a second loop changes the first loop's settings whenever a variable that matters leaves its limits, and keeps changing them until it is back inside.

Ultrastable is that design as working code [3]. For each problem above it uses a specific mechanism:

1. A spec an agent can't misread: each decision logs a prediction that is scored later (DECISIONS-1, `foundation/decisions.py`); the lane's own items now carry a prediction (UNLEARN-DEV-1, `foundation/loopowner.py`)
2. Say what must not be built: standing-rule items say the rule and its probe are out of scope (UNLEARN-DEV-1, `foundation/rules.py`); lane items limit the fix to the pull request's own diff (UNLEARN-DEV-1, `foundation/loopowner.py`)
3. Code that looks right: a merged change is deployed and its verify line is fetched before the item closes (HANDOFF-1, `seed/worker/src/handoff.js`); each claim is tied to a probe (SAY-DO-1, `foundation/saydo.py`)
4. From seems fine to measured: each loop names its closing probe (CLOCKWORK-1, `instances/ultrastable/loop-registry.json`)
5. An agent you can walk away from: trivial changes never open a pull request (SUBSTANCE-1, `foundation/substance.py`); a red main is bisected and the smallest revert applied (RUNWAY-1, `foundation/redmain.py`)

## 3. Putting it into practice

To apply this to your own system, one step per problem:

1. A spec an agent can't misread. Put in place: each decision logs a prediction that is scored later. Check it with one number, share of open work items (docs/issues) that carry both a done check and a checkable prediction, and set a limit for it (>= 0.9 is the limit we use).
2. Say what must not be built. Put in place: standing-rule items say the rule and its probe are out of scope. Check it with one number, share of open work items (docs/issues) that say what the change must not touch (an Out of scope line), and set a limit for it (>= 0.5 is the limit we use).
3. Code that looks right. Put in place: a merged change is deployed and its verify line is fetched before the item closes. Check it with one number, share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit, and set a limit for it (>= 0.95 is the limit we use).
4. From seems fine to measured. Put in place: each loop names its closing probe. Check it with one number, share of registered loops that declare a closing probe and a server-side owner, and set a limit for it (>= 1.0 is the limit we use).
5. An agent you can walk away from. Put in place: trivial changes never open a pull request. Check it with one number, commits on main whose subject starts with Revert, per merged pull request in the window, and set a limit for it (<= 0.05 is the limit we use).

In our own system, 4 of 5 of these checks pass today. Share of open work items (docs/issues) that carry both a done check and a checkable prediction reads 0.235 (n = 17; source: docs/issues/*.json (open items)). Share of open work items (docs/issues) that say what the change must not touch (an Out of scope line) reads 0.588 (n = 17; source: docs/issues/*.json (open items)). Share of uploaded deploys proven live against their commit reads 0.999 (n = 890; source: ops/deploys.jsonl (same window)). Where a check fails, a work item carries the fix, and it closes only when the same check passes.

## 4. Trade-offs and limits

- Scale. One organization: 500 closed pull requests (359 merged) over 7.87 days. Our numbers describe this system; they are not a causal estimate and are not compared with the study's effect sizes as if they were.
- Who wrote the changes. 87% of merged pull requests in the window were opened by code agent sessions run under the owner's account, not by the system's own loops. The latest criticality tick puts the system in the subcritical regime with 0 self-originated deploys, so most of the work measured here was started from outside.
- Review by construction. Ultrastable has no human review step, so a short open-to-merge time is partly a consequence of the design. The real test of the design is quality: the revert and deploy-verification findings, which can fail.
- Revert share counts commits whose subject starts with Revert; a fix that undoes a change without that word is not counted, so the figure is a lower bound.
- Source. Commercial course catalog read as a practitioner source (not peer reviewed; course claims and survey figures are self-reported), version 2026-11-25 (catalog read: 20 live courses, 4 read lesson by lesson); its findings may change in later versions.
